Answer: To Vicki Jones, BE CAREFUL HOW YOU USE YOUR CREDIT CARDS UNTIL YOU CAN GET YOUR CURRENT SITUATION UNDER CONTROL. Immediately determine what your “NEEDS” and “WANTS” (luxuries) are. Be brutal. For example, maybe it’s time to change what you eat, how much you purchase, and where you buy it, as well as your clothes, transportation, entertainment, subscriptions, memberships, vacations, etc. (My sister was trying to advise some people who were always $150 short every month, but they refused to give up their daily $5 Starbucks latte, which would have been an automatic $150 per month savings.) Can you talk to each creditor and work out payment plans? You should at least pay the minimum amount each month, but be prepared to pay a HUGE AMOUNT OF INTEREST when you don’t pay off your cards each month (people with bad credit can be charged as high as 30% annual percentage rates). TRUE STORY: Decades ago, when I worked as the publications manager for a small private college for two years making VERY LITTLE MONEY near Washington, D.C., I changed almost all my habits (I turned the heat way down during the winter, rarely used the air conditioner during the summer, rarely ate out even at fast-food places, ate the all-you-can eat buffet lunch in the college cafeteria for $2.50 [this was the mid 1990s] so I didn’t have to eat much at home, didn’t buy readymade coffee even at 7-Eleven, didn’t buy new clothes, didn’t go on vacations, etc.). When I left that job to take a position as a senior technical editor for a mega corporation making almost three times what I had been making, the financial pressure was off, and I could at long last turn up the heat in the winter and splurge in other ways, but I still retained many of my frugal ways. These days, I try to pay off my credit card bills every month — and often, I pay off the balance every few days so I never get a “surprise” at the end of the month. I also keep track of my expenditures with both my credit cards and my checking account. You can create tables for this in Word or Excel so you are not relying just on their statements. You can also personalize these and add little notes. While I was still working at the college and trying to be frugal, I still found it a challenge to get my spending in line with my limited income. I even met with a financial adviser (a friend, so it was free). He had me write down EVERY PENNY I spent for a couple of weeks, and then he analyzed what I was spending. He couldn’t figure out where I could cut back any more, and he was shocked I was able to cut my spending as much as I did, so it was actually a blessing in disguise when my job at the college ended. I immediately signed on again with a former employer (Creative Options of DC) on a new contract, which led to a 14-year full-time career with Computer Sciences Corporation (CSC). The silver lining. This gave me stability, and (later) a much-appreciated pension.[1] WARNING: Even if you close your credit card accounts, you are still required to pay the debts you owe. DO NOT CLOSE YOUR ACCOUNTS. Question: Can someone withdraw my money from the bank with just an account number?
Answer: To Saba, Yes, someone who is determined, devious, and crafty can steal your money with just your bank account number, but it is not just a simple matter of walking into a bank and asking the teller to hand over your money. Crooks must invest time and patience to pull this off, so you must be situationally aware; do not just wait for your monthly statement to verify what is going on with your bank accounts. Set up immediate notifications of any activity on your accounts! TRUE STORY In 2017, a random stranger wrote a check/cheque to a local grocery store using fake checks he had printed up using my bank’s routing number and my checking account number. The check showed his (or a fake) name and address in a nearby state. My bank’s name was not quite right, but it was close. (Bank routing numbers are public information, and he likely guessed at my account number, because they all fit a certain pattern usually of 8 to 17 digits, no letters.) On different days, he shopped at different stores managed by two local grocery store chains, not national ones like Walmart or Target, and the stores used something called TeleCheck to verify that a check was written on a real checking account. No cashier asked for ID, and he never went to the same physical store twice. If anyone had asked for an ID, he probably had a fake ID that matched the name on the checks. I discovered the first fake check within a day or so, because I monitor my bank account online almost every day. I alerted my bank and filed a police report, and we all decided to leave the account open until we could get a photo of the perp. I contacted corporate headquarters for Weiss Markets and Giant Food, but they refused to do anything. I even called TeleCheck and pleaded with them to stop authorizing any checks on my account, but they refused to do that, so I called them every morning and asked them if they had authorized any more of “my” checks. When they told me they had authorized yet another check on my account, I called USAA (my bank) and told them to reject that check. This went on for about a month. The upshot of it was the crook went all over my county to different stores. Over about a month, he had written over $1,000 worth of checks, usually writing each check for over $100 and getting mostly cash back and purchasing just something small to make it look legitimate. In the end, neither USAA nor I lost any money, because we were on top of this mess. I don’t know whether it was TeleCheck or the individual grocery store chains (Giant Food and Weiss Market) that had to eat the losses, but it was probably TeleCheck. HUGE RED FLAG: I write occasional checks for certain things, but it has been decades since I have written checks at grocery stores (I use credit cards or cash, but not checks), plus I rarely shop at Giant anymore, and I have never shopped at Weiss, so the first bad check was an immediate red flag. I also diligently record which checks I have written, so these fake check numbers did not make sense. EVEN IF I DIDN’T RECORD MY CHECKS, I KNEW I HADN’T SHOPPED AT THOSE STORES. Once we got a photo of the guy through CCTV at some store after he wrote a check, and a screenshot of one of his checks, I closed my account and opened a new one. The guy was already wanted for doing the same thing in Montgomery County, Maryland, with other fake checking accounts, and I am really hoping he was charged with a felony (and convicted!) since the total amount was over $1,000 just from my checking account. He likely was doing this to multiple people, and it was probably a massive criminal operation. NOTE: People can use their regular laser printers at home using official check templates, authorized paper, and special ink to create official-looking checks. (My best friend owns a small inn, and she prints out checks to pay her employees.) I never lost a penny, nor did USAA. I even warned TeleCheck they were dealing with the wrong bank, because USAA is such a bulldog, they would have pursued this matter if it had been just $5. TL;DR — Tell me you are an American without telling me you are an American! Yes, I know checks/cheques are obsolete in most of the world, but I do like to use paper checks for my donations to church, graduation gifts, and an occasional payment to a doctor if they later bill me for a small amount not covered by insurance. These paper check aberrations stood out, because most of my transactions are electronic (credit cards, automatic bill pay, Zelle, and Venmo), and I now have text notifications set up for any amount coming from all of my accounts. —Sarah Madden, #8411, Written and ©Copyrighted ❤️ 15 June 2024 (updated 24 June 2024) QUESTION: Can someone withdraw my money from the bank with just an account number? Question: Should you leave a child without food if they don't like what is offered?
Answer: To Litsa Bolontzakis, Children definitely need to eat, but there is a delicate balance between spoiling children by giving in to every request, forcing them to eat everything, making them starve, and setting reasonable expectations about food. As someone pointed out, a healthy child won’t starve to death by missing one meal. What I did with my two sons was to give them the choice of selecting three items they never had to eat at home. I wrote their choices down for reference. They were probably about six and four years old when I started this, and it continued until they moved out. Meals were far more peaceful this way. I posted “the lists” on the refrigerator, and they were free to change their choices at any time, but not after I had started a meal or made their school lunches. (Liver never had to be on their lists, because it is one of two things on my own “list.”) Before they were even in school, I had become a single mother, and money was tight, so this was a parenting trick I heard about and adopted immediately. Between the two boys, that list included scrambled eggs 🥚 for one, boiled eggs 🥚 for another, mushrooms 🍄, tomatoes 🍅, broccoli 🥦, and tuna fish 🐠. It gave them a sense of control that they wouldn’t be forced to eat certain things, but it also meant I wasn’t their little slave making custom dinners for anyone at the last minute. It also simplified school days when I packed school lunches, and I am sure it saved money in the long run. For example, when I made sandwiches, I made tuna sandwiches for one boy and egg salad sandwiches for the other one. Simple. Years later, the one who wouldn’t eat mushrooms joked that he had “wasted a choice” on mushrooms, because we rarely had mushrooms, which were too expensive. That was the same child who wouldn’t eat tomatoes, and even today as an adult, he will carefully pick tomato chunks out of anything, whether it is a sauce or salad. It’s probably something about the texture or mouth feel. He will gladly eat tomato sauce, but just not the tomato bits. 🍅 The one who wouldn’t eat broccoli as a kid would actually projectile vomit if he ever had broccoli, because it felt like little trees tickling his throat. Now, as an adult, he loves broccoli. 🥦 ALSO, if something wasn’t on the list, they had to at least take three bites of a new food to see if they liked it. They weren’t forced to eat it if they didn’t like it, and there was always something else on the table they could eat. As adults, both sons have become foodies; they love to cook and eat exotic foods, so I am pleased with how everything turned out. My special lists, #8361-A —Sarah Madden, #8361, Written and ©Copyrighted ❤️ 19 May 2024 (updated 20 May 2024) QUESTION: Should you leave a child without food if they don't like what is offered?
